rv.q: In its biggest moments – and there are several – it reaches a delirious kind of excellence.
The musical's creators have fashioned a surprisingly nuanced portrait of a woman who was both victim and enabler of televangelism's excesses.
Katie Brayben gives a powerhouse performance as the televangelism icon, but Elton John's musical struggles to find its spiritual center amid the spectacle.
Ms. Brayben brings both vocal power and emotional nuance to her portrayal of the televangilist, though the musical itself struggles to find the right tone between camp and compassion.
Instead, it's caught in the current of two opposing tides: a straightly-played biopic or satire full of evangelical camp, neither of which are authentically realized.

Those facts aren’t nothing, yet there’s also something about rolling up on Broadway right after the reelection of Donald Trump and expecting to play off decades of nauseating American history with some big yass queen energy that feels simplistic at best, condescending at worst.
Instead, Tammy Faye serves us a likable, sincere gal doing the best she can in a world whose machinations she doesn’t understand.
The problem is that they ended up making her smaller than life.
The songs are undistinguished and unrooted in character, filled with generic and immediately forgettable power ballads, Christian pop tunes and revivalist floor stompers.
“Tammy Faye” feels like it comes from abroad, as indeed it does, because you never believe that any of the creators have any real skin in the game.
Tammy Faye is only slightly more fun than church on a hot July day.
Unfortunately for Sir Elton, the god-awful musical about flamboyant 1980s televangelist Tammy Faye Bakker (later Messner) is a lot more of a “Lestat” than an “Aida.”
Tammy Faye taught us that love wins every time.
Directed by Rupert Goold (Ink, Patriots), this show is a guilty pleasure awash in a colorful struggle between good and evil.

Like its real-life title character, the Elton John musical Tammy Faye isn't flawless. But you must admire its flash, energy, and a bright star turn by Broadway newcomer Katie Brayben in the lead role.
You won’t have a bad time at Tammy Faye, but you probably won’t walk away with a new favorite musical, either.

While Tammy Faye may try to wrap up its lead's life into a pretty bow by preaching about the importance of loving yourself and forgiveness, its end result, sadly, is a complicated portrait of an equally complicated woman.
However, in trying to weave the two topics so tightly together, it doesn’t truly dig into either, instead creating a surface-level, strangely lifeless look at a larger-than-life figure.
But there seems to be no one point of view being conveyed here, a knotty problem that makes for a series of interesting moments, but a less satisfying whole.
But none of the songs amount to much, all style over substance.
Then why is it so unsuccessful as an evening in the musical theater?
The history is fascinating, and this show is not altogether unenjoyable, but Tammy Faye’s creators simply haven’t cracked it.
It isn’t enough (and it’s ultimately patronizing to “the gays”).
We’re expected to find Tammy Faye sympathetic, even though she begs for money from poor people so she can look like a hideously dressed drag queen.
Between those points, well, is anyone keen to see a sad, rather tasteless tabloid musical about good Christian people mostly being bad?
Now comes Tammy Faye, a new, big, loud, high-tech British musical with lots of fury and pumped-up video lavishly applied in a vain effort to create excitement.
Yet for all its promise, “Tammy Faye” struck me as essentially hollow, without a clear reason for existing.
But it’s just like this overblown, condescending, and misguided show to place its heroine on a literal pedestal while also ridiculing her and her beliefs.
“Tammy Faye” fails to celebrate Tammy Faye.

But just as the Bakkers accepted millions of dollars from their true believers and were busted for fraud, it would be hard to justify spending any of your money on this all-around-disappointing musical.

cn.t: Critics find this Elton John musical tonally confused and unfocused, struggling between camp and compassion. While Katie Brayben's performance earns praise, the show is deemed messy, overlong, and unclear about its purpose.

sg.ra: After the 2023 TSX lift the orchestra received wider seats and a slight rake, and center rows G-K are the unobstructed sweet spot before the mezzanine overhang begins at Row K per the official chart; AVFMS reports suggest the overhang only becomes visually noticeable closer to Row N-O, so center G-K is the cleanest post-reno picture.

sg.vl: Discount seats but mezz starts to bite
sg.ra: The mezzanine overhang begins cutting in roughly at Orchestra Row K per the theatre's official seating chart, so rear-orchestra tickets (Row N onward) are priced well below center-premium but you give up the top of the proscenium; one AVFMS reviewer at Row N seat 119 still reported no overhang intrusion, so the rear orch is a real value play on non-spectacle shows that don't use high flying scenery.

Post-2023 lift reviewers specifically call out that the front-mezz sightline is 'incredible' and gives a panoramic view of the choreography, and multiple sources name center Rows A-C (or middle C-F) as the unobstructed sweet spot; avoid the first two side-aisle seats in Row A which Broadway Direct flags as obstructed by a safety railing that survived the renovation.

Unlike most Broadway houses, the Palace rear mezz sits on the same elevated tier rather than under a balcony overhang, so sightlines stay open to the top of the proscenium even at the back — a November 2025 AVFMS reviewer confirmed you are 'pretty high up but atleast you have a full view of the stage'; the tradeoff is distance plus the tight 1920s row spacing the reno preserved.

The Palace's mezz-level boxes are routinely sold as obstructed-view and nytix explicitly warns 'the box seats are not recommended, as they do not provide a clear view of the stage' — the severe side angle means upstage-left blocking is cut off; pick them only if you want the close-in vibe over actually seeing the full stage picture, and never for a dance-heavy or spectacle title.

The balcony survived the lift essentially unchanged — nytix flags that 'the view from the first row of the balcony may be blocked by a large horizontal bar, so sitting in the rows behind the first row is recommended,' and post-reno reviewers still call the balcony 'pretty far' from stage; there is no step-free access, so even the cheapest seat carries real friction.

vr.q: I had a blast. I had an absolute blast from start to finish... don't let the bad word of mouth, especially from the first few previews, deter you from giving this one a shot.
If you wanna have a goofy good time, go see Tammy Faye on Broadway.
so like Tammy Faye herself this musical is very good but slightly flawed I give Tammy Faye four stars
Although I found this pretty easy to sit through, I think for a musical comedy, it is somewhat lacking in the realm of music and comedy.

it's just very confused among itself... we are rarely if ever emotionally captivated by it. The best it can be is charming and sort of charmingly absurd... that I think is the kindest review I can give to Tammy Fay
